750.title: Sabha: Indraprastha
750.hook: a message from a dead father: Pandu, through Narada, asks his son to perform the Rajasuya
750.howItsDone: Hindu families honor their ancestors in shraddha rites, with offerings of food and water, and in the season of Pitru Paksha, when the ancestors are remembered together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the halls of the gods, each known by who sits there. Your line was here is what the sky looks like.

Yudhishthira has been listening closely, and he's noticed something. In Indra's hall, among all the sages and gods, Narada named only one human king: Harishchandra. Not the great kings of Yudhishthira's own line, not the heroes of the old stories. One name. Why him? the king asks. And there's a second question underneath. In Yama's hall, among the dead, you saw my father. You saw Pandu. What did he say?
screen: `ONE KING IN INDRA'S HALL.` → `WHY HARISHCHANDRA?` → `AND MY FATHER?`

segments.voice: Narada answers the first question first. Harishchandra was a mighty king who brought other kings under him and then performed the great sacrifice called the Rajasuya. He gave generously to everyone who came, and because of that sacrifice, he shines in Indra's hall. Then the second answer. Narada had seen Pandu in Yama's hall, and Pandu had seen Harishchandra's place. So Pandu gave Narada a message. Tell my son: you are able to conquer the earth, and your brothers obey you. Perform the Rajasuya. Then I, and our ancestors, may go to Indra's world. Sit with that. Yudhishthira's father died when the brothers were young, back in the forest, and has been gone this whole long serial. Now, in the brand-new hall, in front of everyone, a sage delivers his words. Not comfort. Not, I'm proud of you. A request, and a heavy one. There's something tender in it, though. Pandu is still thinking of his sons, and still thinking of his own fathers before him. A son is asked to do something so that his father can rise with his ancestors. And notice how it reaches him: not as a dream, not as a ghost, but through a guest in the sabha. The hall opened by feeding people is now where the dead can speak to the living. Tomorrow, Narada adds something far less welcome.

751.title: Sabha: Indraprastha
751.hook: Narada adds a warning to Pandu's request and leaves; everyone says yes, and Yudhishthira sends for Krishna
751.carry: send for the one who sees further
751.howItsDone: Hindu tradition remembers Krishna in the Mahabharata as a counselor as well as a god, and his advice to the Pandavas is often retold alongside the story of the Rajasuya.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pandu's words, carried by Narada, asking his son to perform the Rajasuya. Your line was tell my son.

Narada has one more thing to say before he goes. This sacrifice, he tells the king, is hard to finish. It has many obstacles. Brahma-rakshasas, demons who haunt sacrifices, look for any flaw in it. And after it, a war can come that destroys the warriors of the earth. Think it over, Narada says. Do what's good for you. Then he leaves, and the hall is left holding both halves of the message.
screen: `HARD TO FINISH.` → `DEMONS LOOK FOR FLAWS.` → `A WAR CAN COME AFTER.`

segments.voice: A dead father asking his son to rise to this. A sage warning that it might end in ruin. Yudhishthira brushes aside neither. The text says he sighed, and thought, and couldn't find peace. So he does what a king in a sabha is supposed to do: he asks. First his ministers and his brothers. They all say the same thing: you deserve this, the time is right, do it. Then the priests and sages around him, Dhaumya, and Vyasa himself. They agree too. Everyone in the room says yes. And still Yudhishthira doesn't move. The text gives his reasoning. People who love you don't always point out the danger. Some say what pleases. Some are carried along by their own hopes. So he thinks of one person who sees further, who won't flatter him, and who knows the world: Krishna. He sends a fast messenger to Dwaraka, and Krishna comes quickly to Indraprastha. A unanimous yes doesn't end his asking. He isn't looking for a no. He's looking for someone who will tell him the truth, either way. A sabha is a room full of counsel, and the best use of it is knowing whose counsel you most need. This is the last day of the hall's own story. Everything from here leans toward the sacrifice. Tomorrow, Krishna answers.
screen: `A REQUEST AND A WARNING.` · `EVERYONE SAYS YES.` · `LOVE DOESN'T ALWAYS SEE DANGER.` · `SEND FOR THE ONE WHO SEES FURTHER.` · then, large: `A UNANIMOUS YES IS NOT AN ANSWER.`

752.title: the Rajasuya
752.hook: Krishna arrives, hears the plan, and names the one king who stands in the way: Jarasandha of Magadha
752.howItsDone: The Rajasuya belongs to the Vedic royal rites; in the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira's Rajasuya is the rite through which other kings recognize his rule at Indraprastha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: everyone in the sabha said yes, and Yudhishthira sent for Krishna anyway. Your line was send for the one who sees further.
screen: `SEND FOR THE ONE WHO SEES FURTHER.`

segments.voice: Krishna comes straight from Dwaraka, and Yudhishthira lays it all out. My father's wish. The sacrifice. My ministers say yes, my brothers say yes. But you'll tell me the truth: should I perform the Rajasuya? And Krishna does. You have every quality it takes, he says. Then comes the but. There's a king in Magadha. While he lives, this can't be done.
screen: `KRISHNA COMES.` → `SHOULD I DO THIS?` → `YES. BUT THERE'S A KING IN MAGADHA.`

segments.voice: First, what Yudhishthira is asking for. The Rajasuya is the great royal sacrifice, the one Harishchandra performed. A king who completes it is honored by other kings as sovereign over them, so it can't be done alone. Other rulers have to come, and bow, and bring gifts. That's exactly the problem Krishna names. The king is Jarasandha of Magadha. In Krishna's telling, many kings already bow to him. Worse, he has captured kings in battle and holds them shut up in his mountain city, meaning to offer them as a sacrifice to Mahadeva. While those kings sit in his prison, Krishna says, no one else can claim to be honored by the kings of the earth. And Krishna tells it as someone hurt by it. Fearing Jarasandha, he says, my own people, the Yadavas, left Mathura and went to live at Dwaraka. He's not posing as untouchable; he's telling the king plainly what this enemy cost his own family. Look at what his counsel does. It doesn't say yes, and it doesn't say no. It changes the question. Yudhishthira asked, should I perform the sacrifice? Krishna answers: first, what about the kings in that prison? In Krishna's hands the Rajasuya stops being a ceremony for one king's glory and becomes a road through a locked gate. Before anyone can be honored, someone has to be set free. Tomorrow, Yudhishthira very nearly gives the whole thing up.
screen: `A SACRIFICE THAT MAKES A SOVEREIGN.` · `JARASANDHA OF MAGADHA.` · `KINGS LOCKED IN HIS CITY.` · `KRISHNA'S PEOPLE LEFT MATHURA.` · then, large: `FIRST, SOMEONE HAS TO BE SET FREE.`

753.title: the Rajasuya
753.hook: Yudhishthira wants to give the sacrifice up; Bhima and Arjuna argue for it, and Krishna tells how Jarasandha was born in two halves
753.howItsDone: The story of Jarasandha's birth is told in the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, which Hindus read, hear recited and see performed as part of the epic.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya ran into a locked gate: Jarasandha, and the kings in his prison. Your line was a king in Magadha.

Yudhishthira hears about Jarasandha and does something unexpected. He backs down. If even Krishna's people fled from this man, he says, how can we stand against him? Let's give up the sacrifice. Peace is better. It's a startling thing to hear from the man whose father asked for this. Then his brothers speak, one after the other. And Krishna tells a story about how Jarasandha came to be born.
screen: `LET'S GIVE IT UP.` → `THE BROTHERS SPEAK.` → `KRISHNA TELLS A BIRTH STORY.`

segments.voice: Bhima speaks first, and bluntly. A king who never makes an effort, he says, gets worn down like an anthill. Then a plan: Krishna's wisdom, my strength, Arjuna's skill. Together, the three of us can do this. Arjuna argues too: they have the strength and the weapons, so why hold back? Yudhishthira's caution isn't mocked. It's answered. Then Krishna tells where Jarasandha came from. A king of Magadha named Brihadratha had two wives and no son. A sage, Chandakaushika, gave him a single fruit to bring a son. The king divided it between his two wives, so neither would be left out. Each queen gave birth to half a child: one eye, one arm, one leg each. Horrified, the queens had the halves left outside. A rakshasi named Jara found them, and as she picked them up, the halves joined into one strong child. She gave him back to the king. And the text says plainly that his name comes from her: Jarasandha, the one joined by Jara. Why tell this in a war council? The story slows down to show who the enemy is before anyone fights him. And it isn't only a monster's tale. A father who wouldn't leave either wife out. Two mothers who couldn't bear what they saw. A rakshasi who, instead of harming the child, carries him home. Even the enemy has a family story. Tomorrow, the three set out for Magadha, and not dressed as warriors.

754.title: the Rajasuya
754.hook: Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna walk into Jarasandha's city dressed as snatakas, refuse his welcome, and name themselves at midnight
754.carry: they gave their names, and their reason
754.howItsDone: A snataka is a student who has completed Vedic study and taken the ritual bath that ends it; Hindu tradition sets out a snataka's conduct, which is why Jarasandha notices that his guests don't look the part.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Rajasuya nearly given up, then Jarasandha's birth in two halves. Your line was the one joined by Jara.

Three men walk into the capital of Magadha dressed as snatakas, young brahmanas who've just finished their studies. They wear garlands and sandal paste. They don't come in by the main gate, a strange way for students to arrive anywhere. And they walk straight into the king's presence. Jarasandha stands to receive them as honored guests. He has no idea that Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna are standing in his hall.
screen: `DRESSED AS SNATAKAS.` → `NOT BY THE MAIN GATE.` → `THE KING STANDS TO GREET THEM.`

segments.voice: Jarasandha does everything a good host should: water, honors, a seat. They won't take it. Krishna speaks for the group: my two companions are keeping a vow of silence until midnight. Then they'll speak. So the king leaves, comes back at midnight, and asks what he's been holding. Snatakas don't wear garlands and paste like this. Your arms are marked like the arms of men who draw bows. You came in by a wrong way. And you refused my worship. Who are you? Krishna's answer is careful, and honest. A snataka enters a friend's house by its gate, and an enemy's by another way. And we don't accept worship from an enemy. Jarasandha is puzzled: I've never wronged you. Then Krishna names the wrong. You've captured kings and mean to offer them up as a sacrifice. We've come to free them. And he tells the king exactly who they are. The disguise gets them through the door, but once inside they don't hide why they came. They refuse the welcome; some readers say accepting it would have made them guests, and a guest can't rightly fight his host. They wait until he asks, then give their names and their reason. Jarasandha answers just as plainly. I took those kings in war, and I won't let them go out of fear. Fight me, one of you, or two, or all three. He looks the three of them over, and chooses Bhima.

755.title: the Rajasuya
755.hook: Bhima and Jarasandha wrestle for days and nights; the captive kings walk free, and Jarasandha's son is put on his father's throne
755.carry: leave the other side something real
755.howItsDone: In traditional Indian wrestling, kushti, wrestlers train in an akhara, and Hanuman and Bhima are honored there as patrons of strength.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three guests in Jarasandha's hall at midnight, refusing his welcome. Your line was they gave their names, and their reason.

Jarasandha does one thing first. He has his son, Sahadeva, installed as king, so Magadha won't be left without a ruler. A king who holds other kings in chains still makes sure his own people will have someone on the throne. Then he takes off his crown, binds his hair, and steps out to meet Bhima. No armies, no weapons. Two men, bare-handed, and a crowd of citizens gathering to watch.
screen: `HIS SON MADE KING FIRST.` → `NO ARMIES, NO WEAPONS.` → `BHIMA AND JARASANDHA.`

segments.voice: They wrestle, the text says, without stopping for food or rest, day and night, for days on end. They grip and throw. They strike with arms and knees. At last Jarasandha grows tired, and pauses. Krishna sees it and speaks a word to Bhima, who takes it as his signal. He lifts Jarasandha high, whirls him around, and brings him down, and the king of Magadha dies. Here the story could turn into a conquest. It doesn't. The three go straight to the prison and open it. The captive kings walk out and ask Krishna, what can we do for you? His answer is small, almost polite: Yudhishthira wants to perform the Rajasuya. Help him. That's all. Then something smaller. Jarasandha's son, Sahadeva, comes out with his ministers, bowing low, offering gifts. The kingdom is theirs for the taking, and Krishna gives it back. He reassures the young man and installs him as king of Magadha, on his father's throne. Remember where Krishna's counsel pointed: before anyone could be honored, the kings in that prison had to go free. Now look at the order of what he did. Free the prisoners first. Ask them for nothing but help with a rite. Leave the defeated king's family their home. The Rajasuya is still to come, but here is one picture of what it's for, in Krishna's hands.

756.title: the Rajasuya
756.hook: the four younger brothers ride out to the four directions; in the far north, Arjuna reaches a land with nothing to conquer
756.howItsDone: The word digvijaya, conquest of the directions, outlived the epic: tradition uses it for the travels of the teacher Shankara, whose victories are told as debates won across India rather than battles.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a prison opened, and Jarasandha's son put on his father's throne. Your line was leave the other side something real.

Back at Indraprastha, the plan gets bigger. If kings are going to honor Yudhishthira, the brothers will have to go and meet them first. So the younger four divide the world. Arjuna rides north. Bhima rides east. Sahadeva rides south. Nakula rides west. Yudhishthira stays home in the hall, with Dhaumya and his friends around him. Each brother will come back with the tribute of kings. And one will come back from a place where there was nothing to win.
screen: `NORTH, EAST, SOUTH, WEST.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA STAYS HOME.` → `A PLACE WITH NOTHING TO WIN.`

segments.voice: The text follows each brother in turn: kingdoms, battles, and kings who submit or welcome them and send gifts. It's a long march, told region by region. But one moment at its northern edge stands apart. Arjuna rides on, past mountain after mountain, to the land of the Northern Kurus. At the gate, powerful guards stop him, and they speak to him kindly. You can't conquer this place, they say. There's nothing here to fight. Even if you came in, you couldn't see anything with human eyes. We're pleased with you. Tell us what you want. And Arjuna doesn't push. He doesn't try the gate. He says simply: I want my brother Yudhishthira to be sovereign. If this land is closed to humans, I won't enter. Give something as tribute, and I'll go. They give him fine cloth, ornaments and skins, and he turns back. Set it beside the battles around it. The conquest of the directions is about winning recognition for one king. At its far edge, Arjuna, who won Draupadi with his bow, meets a land he can't win, and is content to ask. This week ran from a father's message, through a midnight meeting and a prison opened, to the brothers coming home from four directions with the world's gifts. Everything is ready. Tomorrow, the Rajasuya itself.
screen: `FOUR BROTHERS, FOUR DIRECTIONS.` · `THE NORTHERN KURUS' GATE.` · `NOTHING HERE TO CONQUER.` · `ARJUNA ASKS, AND TURNS BACK.` · then, large: `CONTENT TO ASK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've been pushing at, a door that won't open, and picture yourself at it, the way Arjuna stood at that northern gate. Imagine asking for what you really need, instead of forcing your way in, and let the answer come in its own time. If nothing comes, just rest at the gate.
